title: The Inquisition's Wall
claim: Bernard Délicieux, the friar who led protests against Carcassonne's Inquisition prison, was himself sentenced in 1319 to spend the rest of his life inside it.
explanation: The Inquisition's prison at Carcassonne was called the 'Mur' (the Wall). Its harsher regime, the 'murus strictus', meant a small, dark cell, bread and water, and chains on the feet, sometimes chained to the wall. Townspeople stormed the Wall in 1303 and freed its prisoners, and the Franciscan Bernard Délicieux, the Inquisition's loudest critic, was present. In April 1306 two papal cardinals came to Carcassonne, heard forty prisoners complain of hunger, bad bedding and cruel keepers, and dismissed the jailers. The Inquisition later won. At the end of his trial on 8 December 1319, Délicieux was sentenced to life imprisonment in the inquisitorial prison of Carcassonne, and he died in early 1320.
nuance: The topic hint said '1280s'. The best-documented and verifiable events are 1303–1320, so the claim was moved there. Délicieux's judges ordered his chains and bread-and-water diet waived because of his age and weak hands, but according to Wikipedia Pope John XXII overruled them. The trial's start date is given as 3 or 12 September 1319. Lea's work is 19th-century, though still standard. The 'murus strictus' description is his general account of inquisitorial prisons, not of Carcassonne alone.
visual: A prison building outside the walls of the walled Cité, divided into a milder 'large' wall with corridors and a 'strict' wall of small, dark, separate cells. Archaeologists reported finding its doorway and remains in gardens in front of the ramparts (2014). Its full layout is not known.

sources.supports: Defines murus largus and murus strictus (smallest, darkest cells, chains on the feet, sometimes chained to the wall; bread and water) and says cardinals investigated the Carcassonne prison and eased its rigours.

title: The King's Little Girls
claim: Cardinal Jean Balue spent eleven years locked in one of Louis XI's iron cages.
explanation: The imprisonment is real. Louis XI arrested Cardinal Jean Balue for treason in 1469 and held him until 1480, when the pope secured his release. The cages were real too. Philippe de Commynes, Louis XI's own adviser, describes the king's cruel prisons of iron, or of wood plated with iron. Commynes was held in one of them for eight months, and he was confined at Loches in 1487. But no contemporary evidence puts Balue in a cage. Commynes names Balue's fellow plotter, the Bishop of Verdun, as the first man caged, for fourteen years. The Catholic Encyclopedia calls Balue's cage 'baseless' and says the story began in 16th-century Italy, and the Columbia Encyclopedia calls it 'unproved'.
nuance: The verdict rests on the absence of evidence. Nothing proves Balue was never caged, but no source from his lifetime says he was. Where he was held is also unclear: some accounts say Loches, others the château of Onzain near Blois. The cage shown at Loches today is a reconstruction. The nickname 'fillettes du roi' is traditional, and I did not confirm it in any source I opened.
visual: Commynes describes cages of iron, or of wood covered with iron plates inside and out, too small for comfort. The dimensions of any cage at Loches are not documented in the sources I checked. The cage shown in the Loches keep today is a modern reconstruction.

sources.supports: An eyewitness says Louis XI built cages of iron and iron-plated wood, that the Bishop of Verdun was the first put in one (for fourteen years), and that Commynes himself spent eight months in one. Balue is not mentioned.

title: Dalibor's Fiddle
claim: While imprisoned in the tower in 1498, the knight Dalibor of Kozojedy taught himself the violin, and crowds gathered below to hear him play.
explanation: Dalibor of Kozojedy was real. He was the first prisoner of the new artillery tower at Prague Castle, which was built around 1496, and he was beheaded in 1498 for siding with rebellious serfs on a neighbouring estate. The violin story is legend. Prague's official tourism board points out that the first violins did not reach Bohemia until about a century after his death. The story probably grew out of a saying, 'necessity taught Dalibor to fiddle', which is often read as a grim joke about torture making a prisoner 'sing'. As a nobleman, Dalibor seems to have had a private cell with windows and a stove, and a duller stay than the tales suggest.
nuance: Even the torture explanation is uncertain. A castle guide quoted by Radio Prague says the saying's origin is still unclear and notes that nobles could not legally be tortured. Writers have retold the legend in very different ways, from Jirásek to Smetana's 1868 opera 'Dalibor'.
visual: A round stone artillery tower in the castle's fortifications at the end of Golden Lane. Its lower level served as a dungeon until 1781. Dalibor's own cell is described as private, with windows and a stove.

sources.title: About Daliborka (Legends of Prague)
sources.supports: Tells the legend, then says 'the first violins did not arrive in Bohemia until about a hundred years after Dalibor's execution' and that the saying likely means suffering on the rack forced him to confess.

sources.title: Daliborka: Prague Castle's medieval prison whose first inmate inspired a national legend
sources.author: Thomas McEnchroe
sources.supports: The tower was built around 1496 and Dalibor was its first prisoner, executed in 1498. As a noble he had a private cell with windows and a stove; a guide says the 'fiddle' may be a torture device but the origin is unclear.

place: Old Town Hall (Altes Rathaus), Nuremberg, Franconia, Germany
title: The Hole Under the Town Hall
claim: Prisoners in Nuremberg's 'hole' cells beneath the town hall were usually serving long prison sentences there.
explanation: The Lochgefängnisse (hole prisons) were cut from the vaults of a former bread house when Nuremberg built its town hall in the 14th century. The town hall was also the law court. The city's museums say the cells were reserved mainly for people awaiting trial and people condemned to death. They were a holding pen, not a place to serve a sentence. Prisoners sat in darkness in small wood-lined cells and paid for their own food. In a vault called the 'chapel', they could be tortured to extract confessions, by methods the city court chose. Punishments themselves were usually physical: branding, flogging or execution outside the walls. The sculptor Veit Stoss, held here for forgery, was branded rather than jailed.
nuance: 'Usually' matters. A few people may have stayed longer, but other towers, such as the debtors' tower, served as the city's regular prisons. Most sources available online come from the City of Nuremberg's museum and tourism bodies, which is why confidence is medium. Torture was not abolished in Bavaria until 1813.
visual: A low, vaulted cellar under the Old Town Hall with a row of tiny cells about 2 × 2 m, lined with wooden planks on floor, walls and ceiling. Each held a plank bed, a bench and a board for a table, with a heating basin in winter. There was also a larger vault (the 'chapel') used for torture, plus a forge, kitchen and well room.

title: Little Ease
claim: The Tower of London had a cell called 'Little Ease', so small that a prisoner could neither stand upright nor lie down.
explanation: Little Ease was a real place of punishment. Bishop Challoner's 18th-century martyrology, compiled from contemporary Catholic accounts, records that the priest Stephen Rousham was sent to the Tower in 1582 and 'thrust down into that dungeon, which is called Little Ease', where he was kept for eighteen months and thirteen days. Victorian historians of the Tower describe it the same way. Thornbury's 'Old and New London' says it was 'so small that a prisoner could not stand erect, or even lie down at full length'. De Ros (1866) places a dark cell of that name in the vaults of the White Tower, with a heavy door and no opening for light or air.
nuance: Its exact location and size are uncertain. Sources say beneath the White Tower, but no one knows for sure which space it was, and figures such as '4 feet square' are not well sourced. The tradition that Guy Fawkes was held there in 1605 is unproven, and W. G. Bell (1921) even doubted it held prisoners at all. Other London prisons, such as Bridewell, had their own 'Little Ease'.
visual: A tiny, pitch-dark stone cell in the vaults beneath the White Tower, closed by a heavy door with no window or air vent, and too cramped to stand or lie full length. Its exact dimensions and location are unknown.

place: Veytaux, near Montreux, Lake Geneva, Switzerland
title: The Prisoner of Chillon
claim: François Bonivard spent all six of his years at Chillon chained to a pillar in the lakeside dungeon.
explanation: Bonivard, a Genevan prior who opposed the Duke of Savoy, really was held at Chillon from 1530 until the Bernese freed him in 1536. He was not in the dungeon the whole time. Swiss historians note that for the first two years his noble rank earned him two rooms in the castle. Only when the duke judged this too lenient was he moved underground. Bonivard himself wrote that he was thrust 'into a cell lower than the lake, where I lived four years'. The image of him chained to the fifth pillar comes from Byron's 1816 poem, which Byron subtitled 'A Fable'. Archaeologists have found no trace of a prisoner around the columns.
nuance: Accounts differ: one Chillon guide told swissinfo it was only the last six months in the dungeon, and some sources date the start of his imprisonment to 1532. Bonivard's own claim to have worn a path into the rock floor is literary and unconfirmed. Byron also invented the imprisoned brothers. The historical Bonivard had two brothers, but not as fellow prisoners.
visual: A vaulted Gothic undercroft cut partly from the rock at lake level, with a row of stone columns and windows onto Lake Geneva. Byron's name is carved on one pillar.

sources.title: In the footsteps of the real prisoner of Chillon

title: Cellini's Bedsheet Rope
claim: Jailed in Castel Sant'Angelo, the goldsmith Benvenuto Cellini escaped down a rope made from his bedsheets and broke his leg in the fall.
explanation: In 1538 Cellini was imprisoned in the papal fortress, accused of stealing gems from the papal treasury. In his autobiography he describes cutting his bedsheets into strips and sewing them together. He hid the strips, worked a door off its hinges, climbed onto the roof through the latrines and lowered himself down the central keep. He tied the line to a piece of ancient tile jutting from the wall. Knocked out by a fall from the outer wall, he woke to find his 'right leg was broken three inches above the heel' and crawled into Rome on hands and knees. Independent summaries agree that he escaped with bedsheets, broke his leg and was recaptured, then later released through the Cardinal of Ferrara.
nuance: The escape's details come from Cellini's own boastful memoir, though the imprisonment, escape and recapture are not in doubt. Dates vary: Symonds says Cellini was sent to prison in 1538, while the Catholic Encyclopedia gives 1537–1539. The 'rope' was strips of linen sewn together rather than knotted sheets.
visual: The massive round central keep of Hadrian's former mausoleum, with several stages of high walls below it. Cellini describes climbing to the roof by the latrines and descending on a long band of linen strips rolled on two sticks.

title: The Bottle Dungeon
claim: After Cardinal David Beaton was murdered in his castle in 1546, his killers dumped his body into the castle's bottle dungeon.
explanation: In March 1546 Cardinal Beaton had the Protestant preacher George Wishart burned outside St Andrews Castle. On 29 May 1546 a group of Fife lairds got into the castle disguised as masons and murdered the cardinal. According to Historic Environment Scotland, which cares for the castle, they hung his naked body in a pair of sheets from the castle walls, then threw it into the bottle dungeon in the Sea Tower. HES describes the dungeon as 'a dank and airless pit cut out of the solid rock'. Citing John Knox, it says the body was kept there covered in salt to 'keip him frome stinking'. HES states that the body 'was certainly kept' there.
nuance: Knox's own wording refers to the Sea Tower, and how long the body lay there (weeks or months) and where it was finally buried are uncertain. Wikipedia places the dungeon under the north-west tower. HES and other sources place it in the Sea Tower, which is the north-west tower of the castle. HES says only that Wishart 'may' have been held in the dungeon.
visual: A bottle-shaped pit about 22 ft (7 m) deep, cut into the rock below the Sea Tower. Its only entrance is a narrow neck at the top, opened by a trapdoor in the floor of the tower vault, so prisoners had to be lowered in.
